speaker: Raj
text: What is it, Baba? The little fat girl that used to kick me in the samosas and call me untouchable?

speaker: Mummy
text: Rajesh, do you remember Lalit Gupta? Yes, but now she's a dental student at USC, so we gave her your contact information.

speaker: Raj
text: Why did you do that?

speaker: Baba
text: I don't see your friends. We're twenty-six years old, Rajesh. We want grandchildren.

speaker: Raj
text: But Baba, I'm not supposed to.

speaker: Mummy
text: Lalita's parents approved the match.

speaker: Baba
text: If you decide on a spring wedding, we can avoid monsoon season.

speaker: Raj
text: A spring wedding?

text: It's up to you. They may not want to meddle.

text: If you don't want to meddle, then why are you meddling?

speaker: Sheldon
text: If I may, your parents probably don't consider this meddling. While arranged marriages are no longer the norm, Indian parents continue to have a greater than average involvement in their children's love lives. You seem confused.

speaker: Raj
text: Why are you telling me about my own culture?

speaker: Raj
text: Sorry, Mummy, Baba, but with all due respect, I really can't get you.

text: We have to go. Doogie Howser is on. Baba, it's Doogie time. Bye-bye.

text: I don't believe it.

text: Is it just me, or does web chatting with your clothes on seem a little pointless? Neither do I. Doogie Howser's been off the air for like twenty years.

text: Actually, I read somewhere that it's one of the most popular programs in India.

text: It might speak to a cultural aspiration to have one's children enter the medical profession.

text: What's not to love?

text: Excuse me, hello. My parents are trying to marry me off to a total stranger. What am I going to do?

speaker: Sheldon
text: I suggest you go through with it. Romantic love as the basis for marriage has only existed since the nineteenth century. Up until then, arranged marriages were the norm, and it served society quite well.

text: I'm not a big fan of musicals, but I love that show.

text: Me too. Of course, it speaks to me culturally.

text: Understandable, but there's a universality to that story which transcends ethnicity.
